secondaryFeatures.title: s21e32: Video games are broken; Spotify is less broken; More people have been to Russia...; We actually have an alien?
secondaryFeatures.author: Unknown
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
0.0 Context setting

Thursday 29 September in Portland, Oregon, where it is dreary but also not raining. Dreary kind of implies rain? Some sort of pregnantly dreary, I suppose. Gravid with rain but not raining yet. Anticipatory.

It’s been just over a week since the last episode and I’ve got to say that every day that I haven’t written I’ve gotten more anxious about not having written. This is not generally speaking helpful because I don’t know about you, but it’s easier to write I’m not anxious. Easier to do anything, really.

I can’t remember if I mentioned, but I got invited to speak at Throughline 2027, Active Voice’s online conference. Here’s some stuff about it:

Join me February 3-5 for two days of talks, one day of workshops, and a whole season of special events centered on this year’s theme: ambiguity as opportunity. I’ll be talking about how to stay intentionally human—and humane—in the time of robots. Early-bird tickets are now on sale through November 8. Get all the details at throughlineconf.com/2027.

I mean it says I’m going to be talking about how to stay intentionally human--and humane--but I’m in the middle of tweaking the talk and also trying not to be anxious about that either. The organizers gave me this feedback about my submission:

Is there a weirder, spicier or more personal place you would go? Someplace thinkier, or that takes a long view and explores some of how we got here as a field? That maybe even ruffles some feathers in a productive way?

... which a) thanks, intimidating, b) thanks, flattered, and c) now having thoughts, thanks.

So that’s another Google Doc that’s staring me in the face.

0.1 How People Work, Live!

Last week I had Michele Tepper on and we exchanged some Strong Opinions, which are always fun, and then for me the interesting bit was where we landed on at the end where I think I feel a bit optimistic about how non-developers/product/designers/engineers are vibe-coding things in organizations?

Michele’s episode and all the other ones are up on the podcast and YouTube now; you can catch up on anywhere RSS works with your podcast app, Apple Podcasts, Spotify, and YouTube.

Next up!

Friday 2 October at 9am PT: How People Work, Live! ... with Hillary Hartley

Hillary Hartley has spent nearly three decades helping government be simpler, faster, and better for the people who rely on it. She started out working with 30 state governments at NIC Inc., then went inside as a Presidential Innovation Fellow and co-founder of 18F, the first digital services team in the U.S. government. She later became Ontario's first Chief Digital and Data Officer, where she built the Ontario Digital Service and wrote the Simpler, Faster, Better Services Act. She was also CEO of U.S. Digital Response, a nonpartisan nonprofit helping state and local governments strengthen their tech capacity. She founded OpenPublic to coach public sector leaders and make transformation stick, and she co-chairs the FWD50 conference. She lives in Toronto with her family, their dog, and a veritable zoo of stuffed animals.

And then after that we’ve got:

  • Friday 9 October: HPW, Live! ... with Jim Ray, currently a founding member of developer relations at Bluesky
  • Friday 16 October: HPW, Live! ... with Farrah Bostic, who runs The Difference Engine
  • Friday 23 October: HPW, Live! ... with Lara Hogan, author and coach, and former VP Engineering at Kickstarter and former Director of Engineering at Etsy

Meanwhile, there’s the open How People Work... Does Happy Hour open clinic on Tuesdays at 1pm PT, where you get to bring what you’ve been thinking about and we chat about it as a small group. I’ve run three of these so far and they’ve all been fun.

1.0 Some things that caught my attention

1.1 Video games are broken

In Edge magazine, The game industry is broken – can we fix it?1, there’s an in-depth story covering the current state of the videogame industry. Some bits that caught my attention:

In 2005, Koster studied the previous decade or so of game budgets, and came to a startling conclusion: “The cost of game development goes up about 10x every decade.” In 2017, he repeated the experiment, this time tapping industry contacts to gather numbers on 250 releases spanning over three decades. This larger data set showed him the very same thing. The cost of making a triple-A console or PC game (accounting for inflation) grew from around $1 million in the mid-’90s to $10 million by 2005, and $100 million by 2015. In the blog post accompanying this research, Koster wrote: “We’re talking one-terabyte games that cost $250 million to develop by the early 2020s”. Today, Sweeney talks about “budgets beginning to hit the $250–400 million level” – figures that line up with those in internal documents that leaked from Insomniac in 2023.1

Essentially, games keep getting more expensive to make, but they don’t actually result in more revenue:

“Since around the year 2000, game budgets have literally doubled every few years,” Sweeney says. “The first Gears Of War, in 2006, cost us $12 million to make, and because we sold six million copies on Xbox, we made $100 million. It was immensely profitable. But, by the end of that generation, as we were making [2011’s] Gears Of War 3, it cost about $100 million to make – and our revenue projection was still about $120 million, because the audience wasn’t growing.”1

All that’s true apart from the live service games, where you get a game that regularly and frequently receives content updates and makes money via subscriptions and also in-game purchases. Epic’s Fortnite is an example of this, but in the article it’s clear that Epic isn’t have a good time of it either.

And all of this is against the backdrop of Microsoft seemingly having no coherent strategy for videogames other than (facetiously) “have a videogame console and lose money over time by spending a lot of money”, see The Xbox reset gets ugly2, from The Verge. (Netflix is also trying to figure out what the deal is with videogames because they’re hitting a limit on attention minutes through video, so need to figure out other valuable things to spend your time on for your subscription)

1.2 Spotify is less broken

Hey, that thing I keep complaining about3, where parents or other people looking after kids would have their end-of-year wrap-ups in streaming music services polluted by obsessive kid music (remember The Year of Moana and The Year of Frozen etc etc) because you couldn’t exclude certain genres or artists? They fixed it! Spotify now has a feature that lets you exclude kids and family music from your taste profile4.

Hmm. People have been asking for this for years. I wonder why it suddenly came out? I mean, Spotify have had a whole bunch of other super important strategic things they’ve been working on, like making sure they own the relationship with your ears. And then video podcasts. And all of that jazz. How come they’ve suddenly got time for this? My hunch is that features like the exclude-genres-to-make-parents-more-sane have always been on the backlog (they’re not stupid, after all), they just haven’t been prioritized. So you don’t get to them unless you’ve got capacity and you really start burning through that backlog of stuff to implement.

Anyway it is by pure coincidence that I happened to read about Spotify’s infrastructure for scaling AI coding agents5 last month. You would be unsurprised to learn that Spotify think they’re doing super great at scaling out agentic coding infrastructure:

The organizations that learn fastest, that compound their engineering knowledge into shared, structured systems rather than leaving it scattered across individuals, will be the ones that capture the full value of AI-assisted development. We have proven that pattern at scale. Now we're shipping that expertise to you.5

If you are the kind of person who is trying to avoid using AI-generated/assisted code, I’m afraid we’re in a post-low-background steel environment6, where ever since we started testing nuclear weapons in the atmosphere the background radiation has been, uh “above normal”. (Don’t worry! It is only slightly above normal now, compared to more than slightly above normal!). There’s a bunch of applications where you want steel to, like, not be that radioactive, so it’s been kind of difficult getting hold of it. People started using the low-background steel analogy a few years ago when ChatGPT came out because it came clear that the internet was going to be poisoned forever by LLM-generated material. Surprise! It has been!

1.3 More people have been to Russia than I have

Yeah, that sentence doesn’t make any sense. Sorry if it broke your brain. I discovered comparative illusion/escher sentences a while back and now you get to see them too.

Caught my attention because: you’re kidding, right?

1.4 We actually have an alien?

I am a big fan of the author Max Barry, especially Company, Jennifer Government, and Lexicon, but most recently via Metafilter7 I cam across Barry’s short story It Came from Cruden Farm published by Slate’s future tense8 which you should read because, well. I cannot give it away. But it was fun. And not fun. I won’t say any more.

That’s it for today! I’m clearly finding it a bit harder to write after a very productive spell. But this episode isn’t really what I thought it was going to be about, either. I suppose this is just how the words come out.

How have you been?

Best,

Dan

  7. "The alien [...] and Trump. They didn’t see eye to eye.” | MetaFilter (archive.is), Metafilter, 20 September 2026 ↩

secondaryFeatures.title: The Midterms Are Less Than Two Weeks Away. Make a Voting Plan.
secondaryFeatures.author: Parker Molloy
secondaryFeatures.bodyText:
Earlier this month, the good people over at The Onion released an online game: The Onion Voting Simulator 3D. It’s a retro-style first-person platformer you can play in your phone’s browser (I played through it on my iPhone) or in any desktop browser except Safari.

There are two gameplay options: “Voting Mode” and “Stay At Home Mode.” In “Voting Mode,” the objective is to “cast a ballot and heal democracy.” (No pressure.) In “Stay At Home Mode,” your goal is to “eat a burrito” and “enjoy your digital apartment.” It’s a fun (and funny) way to kill some time. Check it out!

Some of the things you deal with in the voting simulator are things you might encounter in real life. Making sure you’re at the right location, making sure you’ve got whatever forms of ID you need depending on where you live, etc. And… well, there’s a lot of stuff you probably don’t have to worry about (hell demons, a nuclear bomb, a voting machine that functions as a boss fight).

And while it’s good to have a laugh (and I’ll always hype up my pals at The Onion, who do great work), the federal government (i.e., Donald Trump) has been trying to make voting harder and find ways to intimidate voters.

The midterms are less than two weeks away, so if you haven’t figured out what you’ll do if you run into one of the game’s obstacles at your real-life polling place, this weekend is a great time to make a plan.

The administration lost most of its legal fights over voting rules, so it’s leaning harder on intimidation

We all know that Donald Trump is what some might call a “sore loser.” And after his attempted autocoup in 2021 went unpunished — the federal case against him was dropped once he won in 2024 — it makes sense that he’s pushing the envelope (a bit of an understatement) when it comes to trying to tilt the midterms in his favor.

Since retaking office in January 2025, Trump has signed two executive orders on voting. Judges blocked most of the first one, from March 2025. The second tried to control how the Postal Service delivers mail ballots, and the Supreme Court made sure that rule won’t apply this November. The Department of Justice has also filed 31 lawsuits trying to get its hands on voter rolls. Thankfully, by the Brennan Center’s tally, it’s 0-for-26 in the ones judges have ruled on so far. Then there’s the SAVE America Act, which would make people show documentary proof of citizenship to register and photo ID to vote. It’s stuck in the Senate.

So, yes, Trump is trying to interfere, which should be treated as a gigantic scandal in itself. But he’s hit some bumps in the road. Those bumps are good.

After a summer of court fights over Trump’s mail-ballot order, NPR summed up where things landed: “In the end, no mail voting rules have actually changed.” That hasn’t kept people from worrying. Carly Koppes is a Republican election official in Colorado’s Weld County, and she told NPR she’s been hearing from confused voters. “This is my 22nd year [running elections],” she said. “Absolutely, this is the most uncertain.”

That uncertainty didn’t come from nowhere. Asked in May whether federal agents might be sent to polling places, Trump said he’d do “anything necessary” to make sure elections are “honest.” Last month, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, said ICE might come to a polling place to serve a warrant, and FBI Director Kash Patel wouldn’t rule out his agents showing up at the polls either, offering only that they’d “follow the law.” DHS told NPR that ICE “is not planning operations targeting polling locations,” and then, in the very next line:

“ICE conducts intelligence-driven targeted enforcement, and if an active public safety threat endangered a polling location, they may be arrested as a result of that targeted enforcement action.”

It also said, “Those who are here legally and are not breaking other laws have nothing to fear.”

Then there’s the Justice Department. It plans to send about 1,000 monitors to the polls this year, which Harmeet Dhillon, who runs its Civil Rights Division, called “the largest monitoring effort” DOJ has ever run (roughly three times as many monitors as it sent for the last midterm). This time, it also plans to use some criminal prosecutors, which the department used to avoid because of how that might feel to voters. The NAACP is in court trying to keep prosecutors, and law enforcement generally, out of the monitor ranks. Kiersten Pels, a DOJ spokesperson, argued that the lawsuit grew out of “unwarranted fear and baseless speculation.” She also said this, which I assume was meant to be reassuring:

“Monitors will not identify themselves as prosecutors.”

In California, the department is suing to make the state set aside the ballots of anyone on a list of about 20,000 people it calls “likely” noncitizens, and the administration has warned election officials that if they knowingly count those ballots, they “risk becoming aiders and abettors to a federal crime.” When Los Angeles County did a preliminary review of 200 names from the list, 38.9% of the people whose birthplace was “meaningfully reported” listed a U.S. one. Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, had already conceded at a Monday press conference that the list might not be clean: “There may be some names on there who it turns out ultimately are citizens, we’re not perfect,” he said. “And that’s why we’ve asked California to cooperate with us.”

Is any of it landing? Yeah. Even before most of that, a UC San Diego poll taken Sept. 1-9 found that about 40% of Americans thought it was likely ICE agents would be at voting sites near them, and the worry that immigration agents would question them, even though they’re citizens, was much higher for people of color than for white people.

And that’s kind of the idea, right? If the administration can make voters so afraid that they’ll be harassed or intimidated by Trump goons at the polling place that they stay home, then it has accomplished its goal, no goons required.

Share

So make a plan

Have you ever made a voting plan before? You should! Here’s a good place to start. (If you want an even longer checklist, Ms. has a good one, which I leaned on here.)

If you’ve got a few moments this weekend, you should check your registration, find your polling place and its hours, and look up exactly what sort of ID you need to cast a ballot (VoteRiders has a state-by-state rundown).

If you’re voting by mail, consider hand-delivering your ballot to either your election office or an official drop box (if your area has them) instead of putting it in the mail. The Postal Service recommends mailing it at least a week before your state’s deadline. Most states won’t count a ballot that arrives after Election Day, whatever the postmark says, and several more have adopted that rule since the last midterms.

If you’re told by a poll worker that your ID isn’t acceptable, ask what you can do. In some states, you can sign a sworn statement and vote as you normally would. In other, stricter states, you might be allowed to cast a provisional ballot that will count if you do something like show your ID at an election office within a specific window of time. Basically, now’s the time to check to see what you need. If you don’t have an acceptable ID, VoteRiders will help you get one for free (call or text 866-432-8683).

If they can’t find your name at the polling place, ask them to double-check that you’re in the right place (in many states, a provisional ballot cast at the wrong precinct won’t count). Have them direct you to the correct location. Around 20 states and D.C. let you register and vote on Election Day itself, which can clear up this problem, too. For everyone else, you can ask for a provisional ballot. Ask what you need to do for it to count, and by when.

As for anyone at the polls who isn’t a poll worker, you don’t owe them a conversation. Some states, including Florida and Texas, bar partisan poll watchers from talking to voters at all. DOJ monitors can watch, and they can talk to you once you’re outside, Reuters reports, but they have no power to open an investigation right there or keep anybody from casting a ballot. In most states, they can’t come inside without election officials’ permission, and DOJ has agreed under administrations of both parties that its monitors will openly say they’re monitors.

An agent stopping you is a different situation. The Brennan Center’s guide for voters says to ask if you’re allowed to leave, and if they say yes, to go, calmly. You don’t have to answer their questions (in some kinds of stops, like traffic stops, you may have to identify yourself), and without a warrant, you don’t have to unlock your phone for them. It’s also against federal law for anyone, government officials included, to “intimidate, threaten, or coerce” you for voting. If you see that happening, to you or anybody else, tell the poll workers (or whoever’s in charge there), call or text Election Protection, and, if you can do it safely, write down what happened and when. Anyone in danger? Call 911.

One more thing: don’t post that ICE is at your polling place unless you know it is. Brennan warns that a false report can scare people out of voting by itself.

And if there’s still a line when your polling place closes, don’t leave it. If you got in line before closing, you get to vote.

For anything else, there’s the Election Protection hotline, run by a nonpartisan coalition, administered by the Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights Under Law and answered by trained volunteers. Put these in your phone now:

  • 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683), call or text

  • 888-VE-Y-VOTA (888-839-8682) in Spanish

  • 888-API-VOTE (888-274-8683) in Asian languages

  • 844-YALLA-US (844-925-5287) in Arabic
